title: “MY BELOVED IS TO ME A SACHET OF MYRRH BETWEEN MY BREASTS”: Yes, That Image Is in the Bible
paragraphs: “MY BELOVED IS TO ME A SACHET OF MYRRH BETWEEN MY BREASTS”: Yes, That Image Is in the Bible

Song of Songs 1:13 contains one of Scripture’s most intimate images—and beneath its startling beauty is a truth about love, longing, nearness, and ultimately the Savior who came close enough to carry our shame.
There are Bible verses people put on coffee mugs.
There are Bible verses stitched onto pillows.
There are verses quoted at graduations, printed beneath sunsets, and posted whenever somebody needs encouragement.
And then there is Song of Songs 1:13.
“My beloved is unto me as a bundle of myrrh, that lieth betwixt my breasts.”
Yes.
That is in the Bible.
And before somebody nervously turns the page, makes a joke, or wonders why God allowed language this intimate into Holy Scripture, perhaps we should do something increasingly rare.
Perhaps we should let the Bible speak without being embarrassed by it.

Because what appears at first to be a startling sentence about a woman, her beloved, perfume, and her breasts becomes something deeply beautiful when we slow down long enough to hear what the Hebrew is actually saying.
The Hebrew reads:
צְרוֹר הַמֹּר דּוֹדִי לִי בֵּין שָׁדַי יָלִין
Tseror hammor dodi li, bein shadai yalin.
Literally, the sense is something like:
“A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me; between my breasts he spends the night.”
The language is intimate.
There is no honest reason to pretend otherwise.

The Song of Songs celebrates the powerful affection, desire, delight, exclusivity, beauty, and longing between a man and a woman. Scripture does not treat marital love as something filthy that God reluctantly tolerates. The God who created humanity male and female also created covenant intimacy, and within its God-given boundaries Scripture can speak about that intimacy with a poetic freedom that sometimes makes modern religious people more uncomfortable than the Bible itself seems to be.
But look more closely.
She is not describing a sexual act.
She is describing precious nearness.
Myrrh was aromatic and valuable. A small bundle or sachet of it could be worn close to the body, allowing its fragrance to remain with the wearer.
That changes the picture.
Her beloved is so precious to her that she compares him to fragrance kept against her heart.
Close.
Treasured.
Remembered.
Carried.
His presence remains with her.
Even when he is not physically there, the fragrance reminds her of the one she loves.
And suddenly an ancient love poem begins asking a painfully modern question:
What are you carrying closest to your heart?
Not what do you post about.
Not what Bible verse is in your bio.
Not what worship song is playing in your car.
What actually lives near your heart when nobody is watching?
Because everybody carries something there.
Some carry the memory of someone who wounded them.
Some carry the name of someone who left.
Some carry an addiction they have learned to hide beneath Christian vocabulary.
Some carry resentment.
Some carry pornography.
Some carry ambition.
Some carry the desperate need to be admired.
Some carry grief so quietly that even the people sitting beside them in church have no idea they are barely surviving.
Some carry shame.
Old shame.
The kind that learned your address years ago and never seemed to move out.
Maybe that is why this strange little verse can become so unsettling.
“My beloved…”
Not merely my doctrine.
Not merely my denomination.
Not merely my religious identity.
My beloved.
There is an enormous difference between knowing information about somebody and loving them.
And there is an enormous difference between knowing Christianity and knowing Christ.
You can know when to raise your hands.
You can know when to say amen.
You can know Christian language well enough that nobody suspects anything.
You can serve.
Preach.
Sing.
Post Scripture.
Defend theology.
Win arguments.
And still discover, in the silence of midnight, that Jesus has been living at the edges of your life instead of at the center of your affection.
That is where this verse becomes dangerous.
Because love always exposes our treasures.
Jesus said, “For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” (Matthew 6:21).
Your heart eventually reveals what you believe is precious.
And the woman in the Song essentially says:
My beloved is precious enough to keep near my heart.
Now we need to be careful.
Song of Songs 1:13, in its immediate literary setting, is love poetry. We should not erase that meaning or pretend every reference to the bridegroom is secretly a coded prediction about Jesus.
But Christians have long recognized that Scripture also gives us a greater Bridegroom-and-bride pattern.
The New Testament explicitly presents Christ as the Bridegroom and His people as His bride.
Jesus identifies Himself with bridegroom imagery in the Gospels.
Paul writes of Christ and the church in Ephesians 5.
Revelation moves toward the marriage supper of the Lamb.
So without destroying the original meaning of Song of Songs, the language of beloved, longing, covenant love, and intimate nearness can awaken a larger biblical meditation:
What does it mean for Jesus Christ to become precious to us?
Not useful.
Precious.
Not an emergency contact when life collapses.
Beloved.
Because Christianity begins becoming unrecognizable when Christ Himself stops being its treasure.
And perhaps somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You did not wake up one morning and announce, “Today I will become spiritually cold.”
It happened quietly.
One compromise.
One disappointment.
One unanswered prayer.
One secret.
One wound you never processed.
One Sunday missed.
Then another.
The Bible remained on the table.
Prayer became shorter.
Conviction became easier to silence.
Things that once disturbed your spirit became entertainment.
Things you once prayed against became things you learned to excuse.
And somehow Jesus went from being the One you could not stop talking about…
to the One you rarely talk to.
Yet here is where the Gospel interrupts the story.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of humanity desperately climbing toward God.
It is the story of God coming down.
“The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).
Think about that.
The Holy One came near.
The Creator entered His creation.
The eternal Son took on flesh.
Jesus did not save sinners from a comfortable distance.
He walked dusty roads.
He touched lepers.
He ate with people respectable society despised.
He received the broken.
He confronted hypocrites.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He wept.
He bled.
He was betrayed.
He was mocked.
He was stripped.
He was crucified.
And here the image of myrrh becomes even more haunting.
Because myrrh does not disappear after Song of Songs.
Myrrh appears again around Jesus.
The Magi brought gold, frankincense, and myrrh to the child Jesus (Matthew 2:11).
At Golgotha, Jesus was offered wine mingled with myrrh, which He did not take (Mark 15:23).
And after His death, Nicodemus came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes for His burial (John 19:39).
The myrrh of biblical poetry therefore carries associations that stretch from fragrance and costly beauty into suffering and burial.
We should not force those passages into an artificial code. Scripture deserves better than clever connections pretending to be exegesis.
But once you have seen myrrh beside the beloved in the Song…
and then smelled myrrh again near the crucified and buried Christ…
it is difficult not to feel the weight of the biblical imagery.
The Christian faith says the Beloved came near enough to die.
Near enough to enter our suffering.
Near enough to bear sin.
Near enough to be laid in a tomb.
Near enough that guilty people no longer have to run from God.
And maybe that is what someone reading this needs to hear tonight.
You have spent years believing Jesus would love the cleaned-up version of you.
So you kept hiding the real one.
The angry one.
The addicted one.
The ashamed one.
The jealous one.
The exhausted one.
The one who keeps returning to the same sin and wondering whether repentance is still possible.
The one who knows how to look victorious on Facebook while privately falling apart.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not an invitation to make peace with sin.
Jesus does not call darkness light.
Grace does not mean rebellion no longer matters.
Christ calls sinners to repentance.
But repentance is not cleaning yourself before approaching Jesus.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior because you finally realize sin cannot give you what it promised.
Jesus said He came to call sinners to repentance (Luke 5:32).
That means your scandal does not shock Him.
Your history does not confuse Him.
Your hidden chapter was never hidden from Him.
He already knew.
And still the cross happened.
That is scandalous grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that pats sin on the head and tells it to stay.
Grace that finds sinners where they are and refuses to leave them there.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that confronts.
Grace that cleanses.
Grace that teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace that takes people who were spiritually dead and makes them alive in Christ.
Maybe you thought your greatest need was for God to improve your reputation.
No.
You need resurrection.
You need forgiveness deeper than your shame.
You need righteousness you could never manufacture.
You need a Savior.
And His name is Jesus.
This is where Song of Songs 1:13 stops being merely the Bible verse that made you raise your eyebrows.
It begins asking where your deepest affection rests.
“My beloved is to me…”
Can you say that about Christ?
Not because you have performed perfectly.
Not because your faith has never trembled.
Not because you never struggle.
Peter loved Jesus and still denied Him.
Thomas belonged to Jesus and still wrestled with doubt.
The disciples followed Jesus and still fled when fear became unbearable.
The Bible is full of people whose devotion was painfully human.
But Jesus kept rewriting stories.
Peter's denial was not the final sentence.
Thomas's doubt was not the final sentence.
The disciples' fear was not the final sentence.
The cross itself looked like the final sentence.
Then Sunday morning came.
The stone moved.
The tomb emptied.
Death lost its claim.
Jesus Christ rose.
And that is why your worst chapter does not have to become the title of your life.
Your sin may explain part of your past.
It does not have to own your future.
Your failure may be true.
Grace is also true.
Your wounds are real.
The resurrection is real.
Your repentance may begin with tears.
But those tears can fall at the feet of a living Savior.
This is what we mean when we say:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not because Jesus edits history until sin no longer matters.
He does something infinitely greater.
He redeems sinners.
He takes the guilty and justifies them by grace through faith.
He takes enemies and reconciles them.
He takes prodigals and brings them home.
He takes hearts crowded with lesser loves and teaches them again to say:
My Beloved.
Maybe you have been carrying shame between your heart and everything else for years.
Maybe tonight it is time to carry a different fragrance.
The remembrance of Christ.
His cross.
His mercy.
His words.
His wounds.
His empty tomb.
His promise that everyone who comes to Him will not be cast out.
You do not need another performance.
You need surrender.
You do not need to convince everybody online that you are okay.
You need Jesus.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, do not manufacture a polished religious response.
Be honest.
Somebody reading silently may need evidence tonight that grace still reaches people in real life.
Then think of one person.
You already know who it is.
The friend whose posts have changed lately.
The brother who stopped attending church.
The daughter who says she is fine but does not sound fine.
The believer quietly drifting.
The person who thinks Christianity is only condemnation and has never really understood the cross.
There are truths we understand differently when midnight comes.
There is another way you can help this ministry continue.
Not through pressure.
Not by purchasing God's favor.
And we will not tell you that paying us earns a blessing from God.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Jesus already paid the price we could never pay.

But Scripture does affirm the material support of Gospel ministry. Paul writes that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living from Gospel work (1 Corinthians 9:14), while also teaching that Christian giving must come from the heart rather than manipulation or compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Think of it as an offering of support for the mission—not a payment to God, not the purchase of salvation, and not something we will falsely declare to be your biblical tithe.
But hear this clearly.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
Salvation is by grace.
The cross is enough.
Repent and believe the Gospel.

And if God has given you resources and you desire to glorify Him through generosity, ask Him where and how you should give. Support your local church and faithful Gospel work. Help people in need. Give freely. Give wisely. Give cheerfully. If Gospel Warrior is one of the ministries you choose to support, we will receive that support with gratitude and use it to help continue the mission.
Because perhaps the greatest tragedy would be to spend our lives keeping everything except Christ close to our hearts.
Money close.
Approval close.
Resentment close.
Secret sin close.
Old wounds close.
The opinions of strangers close.
Our phones close.
Our image close.
Our pride close.
And Jesus somewhere at the edge.
The woman in the ancient Song knew the language of treasured nearness:
“My beloved is unto me as a bundle of myrrh…”
What would happen if Christ became that precious to us?
What would happen if the first name our hearts reached for in suffering was Jesus?
What would happen if repentance stopped feeling like humiliation and began feeling like coming home?
What would happen if we stopped protecting the scandal and finally surrendered it to grace?
Maybe heaven is not asking you tonight for a better mask.
Maybe Christ is calling you to come into the light.
Wounded.
Ashamed.
Repentant.
Empty-handed.
But coming.
And when you come to Jesus, you discover something astonishing.
The Savior you thought would recoil from your scars is the Savior who shows you His.
So share this if somebody needs to hear it.
And comment something real.
Not something impressive.
Something real.
“Jesus, bring me back.”

Because somewhere beneath all the noise, all the failure, all the religious performance, all the wounds, and all the things you wish you could undo, there is still a Savior calling sinners out of darkness.
And perhaps the sentence you thought ended your story was only the place where Jesus picked up the pen.
Your scandal may be part of the story—but when Christ holds the pen, your scandal does not get the final word.
